### Atherton v. Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, 519 U.S. 213 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** January 14, 1997.

#### Judgment

Vacated and remanded, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The court of appeals shall direct application of New Jersey law, subject to § 1821(k)’s federal gross-negligence minimum. Breach, causation, defenses, and available relief remain for the lower courts.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Breyer | Stone, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg in full; O’Connor, Scalia, and Thomas except the legislative-history discussion | Supports vacatur and remand | Complete opinion for six Justices; all portions except legislative history for three |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | O’Connor | Scalia and Thomas | Supports vacatur and remand | Relies on statutory text and structure without legislative history |

#### Question 1: Governing law and § 1821(k)

**Question decided:** Governing law and § 1821(k).

**Holding:** State law ordinarily governs the duty of care owed by officers and directors of a federally chartered savings association. Section 1821(k) establishes gross negligence as a minimum federal basis for liability and preserves stricter applicable state standards.

**Controlling explanation:** A State may impose liability for simple negligence or another standard more demanding than gross negligence. State law may not insulate officers and directors from the federal gross-negligence minimum. Federal chartering, insurance, supervision, or receivership convenience does not by itself authorize a federal common-law ordinary-negligence rule.

The asserted duties concern lending judgment, fiduciary administration, and corporate governance, subjects traditionally governed by state law. The FDIC identifies no operational conflict requiring displacement. Section 1821(k)’s preservation clause would perform little work if the statute were treated as a ceiling, while reading it as a floor gives effect to both the gross-negligence language and the preservation of rights under other applicable law.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not determine New Jersey’s business-judgment rule, whether Atherton breached any duty, or the standard governing a distinct federal enforcement action based on duties created by federal statute or regulation.

**Legal basis:** 12 U.S.C. § 1821(k), federal-common-law principles, and applicable state corporate law.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Breyer, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *O’Melveny & Myers v. FDIC* is applied and clarified. Its state-law presumption governs traditional corporate duties even when the failed institution was federally chartered. Section 1821(k) supplies a specific federal minimum without displacing stricter state standards.

### Elizabeth G. Curtis v. School Committee of Falmouth, 420 Mass. 749, 652 N.E.2d 580

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** January 21, 1997.

#### Judgment

Affirmed, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

Justice Kennedy delivered the Opinion of the Court, joined by every participating Justice.

#### Question 1: Parental liberty and familial privacy

**Question decided:** Parental liberty and familial privacy.

**Holding:** A voluntary public-school condom-availability program does not violate parental liberty or familial privacy merely because it contains no parental opt-out or notification requirement.

**Controlling explanation:** Parents retain primary authority to instruct their children on morality, religion, and sexual conduct. The State does not constitutionally displace that authority by making a nonprescription preventive item available when students need not obtain it, receive counseling, read materials, affirm a message, or suffer any consequence for refusing.

The program changes what is available at school, not the family’s legal relationship or the parents’ authority to instruct their children. Compulsory attendance does not make every optional school resource compulsory. A parent’s instruction may become more difficult when the school presents an option the parent rejects, but difficulty and offense are not coercive governmental interference.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not decide confidential medical treatment, prescription medication, compelled sex education, distribution to a child legally unable to consent, or a program that penalizes adherence to parental instruction.

**Legal basis:** Fourteenth Amendment.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Kennedy, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

#### Question 2: Free exercise

**Question decided:** Free exercise.

**Holding:** The program imposes no substantial burden on religious exercise because neither students nor parents are required to approve, obtain, or use condoms, and no educational benefit or disciplinary consequence depends on participation.

**Controlling explanation:** The Constitution protects against coerced religiously prohibited conduct and targeted disability. It does not require removal of every voluntary public program inconsistent with a person’s faith.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision does not govern religious targeting, compelled participation, or denial of an exemption from a mandatory practice.

**Legal basis:** Free Exercise Clause.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Kennedy, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** The decision creates the first controlling simulated rule concerning voluntary school access to nonprescription preventive items. *A. St. P. C.* and *Baby Richard* remain confined to state action altering or implementing legal family status.

### Ingalls Shipbuilding, Inc. v. Director, Office of Workers’ Compensation Programs, 519 U.S. 248 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** February 18, 1997.

#### Judgment

| Judgment component | Disposition | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Relief or remand |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Predeath settlement and § 33(g) forfeiture | Affirmed, 9-0 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | None | Mrs. Yates’s later death-benefit claim is not barred by the predeath settlements. |
| Director as respondent | Affirmed, 7-2 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Scalia, Thomas | The Director may remain as the Department’s designated representative. |

The amount of benefits, work-related causation, and any other defenses remain for the agency process.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | O’Connor | Every Justice as to the compensation issue; Stone, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer as to Director participation | Supports affirmance | Unanimous on compensation; seven-Justice Court opinion on participation |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Scalia | Thomas | Supports the compensation judgment and opposes the participation ruling | Rejects the Director’s status as Rule 15(a) respondent |

#### Question 1: Predeath spouse and § 33(g)

**Question decided:** Predeath spouse and § 33(g).

**Holding:** An injured worker’s spouse is not a “person entitled to compensation” for LHWCA death benefits before the worker dies from a qualifying cause. A predeath third-party settlement therefore does not trigger § 33(g)’s approval forfeiture for the later death-benefit claim.

**Controlling explanation:** Entitlement is assessed when the settlement is made. A contingent possibility of future widowhood is not present legal entitlement, because the spouse may predecease or divorce the worker, or the worker may die from a nonqualifying cause.

The statute uses entitlement, not expectancy. The phrase “would be entitled” compares settlement value with compensation after the legal prerequisites for entitlement exist; it does not convert every potential future beneficiary into a present claimant. General concern about double recovery cannot add a forfeiture Congress did not enact.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not govern settlements entered after the worker’s death, vested disability benefits, or offsets expressly authorized elsewhere.

**Legal basis:** 33 U.S.C. §§ 909 and 933.

**Authority:** Unanimous.

#### Question 2: Director as respondent

**Question decided:** Director as respondent.

**Holding:** The Director of OWCP, acting as the Secretary’s designated representative of the Department of Labor, is a proper respondent under Rule 15(a) when a private party has invoked appellate jurisdiction to review a Benefits Review Board order.

**Controlling explanation:** The Board, administrative law judges, and Director perform different functions within the Department. The Board’s order is the Department’s order, and the Secretary may designate the Department’s appellate representative. Respondent status permits the Director to state the Department’s position, including disagreement with the Board, without giving the Director an independent right to initiate an appeal.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not reconsider *Newport News* or decide whether the Director alone can preserve an Article III controversy after all private adversity ends.

**Legal basis:** Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 15(a), 33 U.S.C. § 921a, and Department regulations.

**Authority:** O’Connor’s opinion, joined on this issue by Stone, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer, supplies a seven-Justice majority.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Director, OWCP v. Newport News Shipbuilding & Dry Dock Co.* is distinguished. Its restriction on the Director’s initiation of review does not prevent respondent participation after a private party invokes appellate jurisdiction.

### Uhlrig v. Harder, 64 F.3d 567

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** February 18, 1997.

#### Judgment

Affirmed, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Breyer | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg | Supports affirmance | Constitutional merits and judgment |
| Concurrence in the judgment | Scalia | Thomas | Supports affirmance | Would resolve the damages action on qualified immunity without extending substantive due process |

#### Question 1: State-created danger

**Question decided:** State-created danger.

**Holding:** The record does not establish the affirmative inducement, material increase in vulnerability, deliberate indifference, and defendant-specific causation required by *Pinder*.

**Controlling explanation:** Closing the secure unit and delegating reassignment were affirmative policy decisions, but the named senior officials did not give Uhlrig a concrete assurance of safety, induce her to abandon a protective course, conceal Waddell’s history, or personally direct his placement into her care. The warnings, access to records, and delegated clinical process prevent the policy decision from becoming the particular affirmative sequence recognized in *Pinder*.

**Application:** Summary judgment is proper because no reasonable factfinder could attribute the constitutionally required inducement and causal sequence to the named defendants. The Court therefore does not reach qualified immunity as to the seven-Justice merits coalition.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision does not protect an official who conceals a known imminent threat, promises safety and then directs an employee into the identified danger, or personally overrides safeguards with deliberate indifference.

**Legal basis:** Fourteenth Amendment and 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

**Authority:** Breyer’s opinion, joined by Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg, supplies a seven-Justice majority.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Pinder v. Johnson* is applied without alteration. The decision confirms that an affirmative institutional policy change is not enough by itself; the claimant must prove the defendant-specific sequence of inducement, increased vulnerability, culpability, and causation required by *Pinder*.

### Auer v. Robbins, 519 U.S. 452 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** February 19, 1997.

#### Judgment

Affirmed, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The officers remain classified as exempt executives, subject to reimbursement and prospective compliance required by the correction provision.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Scalia | Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer in full; Stone as to the regulation’s public-sector validity and the duties determination | Supports affirmance | Eight-Justice Court opinion on own-regulation deference; unanimous result on validity and exemption |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Stone | None | Supports affirmance | Independently construes the regulation and rejects automatic controlling deference |

#### Question 1: Validity of the salary-basis regulation

**Question decided:** Validity of the salary-basis regulation.

**Holding:** The salary-basis condition is a permissible implementation of the FLSA executive exemption as applied to public employees.

**Controlling explanation:** Congress gave the Secretary broad authority to define and delimit the exemption. A rule distinguishing fixed salary from compensation varying with work quantity or quality remains reasonably related to executive status despite the disciplinary needs of public-safety organizations.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Any procedural objection to the Secretary’s failure to amend the regulation after public employees became subject to the FLSA must be presented through the appropriate rulemaking process.

**Legal basis:** 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(1) and the then-effective regulations.

**Authority:** Unanimous.

#### Question 2: Interpretation of an agency’s own regulation

**Question decided:** Interpretation of an agency’s own regulation.

**Holding:** When ordinary interpretation leaves an agency regulation genuinely ambiguous, the agency’s authoritative interpretation controls unless it is plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation, provided it reflects the agency’s fair and considered judgment rather than a convenient post hoc rationalization.

**Controlling explanation:** An interpretation may receive controlling weight even when presented in an amicus brief if it states the agency’s established, authoritative position and is not manufactured to defend the particular litigation. Deference cannot make the regulatory text bear a meaning it cannot reasonably carry.

“subject to reduction” comfortably permits a practical-exposure interpretation. The Secretary’s position reflects the agency’s administration of its own salary-basis rule and does not arise as an unexplained litigation invention.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not authorize deference to an inconsistent, secret, plainly erroneous, or merely convenient interpretation.

**Legal basis:** The regulation and the received *Seminole Rock* principle.

**Authority:** Scalia’s opinion, joined on this question by Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer, supplies an eight-Justice majority. Stone does not join this proposition.

#### Question 3: Salary status, correction, and duties

**Question decided:** Salary status, correction, and duties.

**Holding:** An employee is “subject to reduction” when an actual practice of inconsistent deductions exists or a clear and particularized policy creates a significant practical likelihood of such deductions. The general St. Louis manual and isolated deduction do not defeat salary status here.

**Controlling explanation:** An employer may preserve exempt status by reimbursing an improper deduction and committing to future compliance when the deduction was inadvertent or was made for a reason other than lack of work.

Theoretical disciplinary authority is not enough. The manual did not communicate a recurring compensation practice specific to these officers, and the record showed no pattern of inconsistent reductions. Their undisputed supervisory responsibilities satisfy the executive-duties requirement.

**Limits and questions not reached:** A recurring deduction practice or a clear policy specifically threatening salary reductions for ordinary work variations would present a different case. The separately asserted evidentiary-burden argument is not reached because it was not adequately preserved.

**Authority:** Scalia’s opinion and Stone’s concurrence support the practical-exposure construction, correction mechanism, and case-specific exemption at the same operative level. Those propositions are unanimous, although the rationale concerning agency deference is not.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** The question reserved in *Thomas Jefferson University v. Shalala* is resolved. Eight Justices adopt controlling own-regulation deference when genuine ambiguity remains and the interpretation satisfies the limits stated above. Stone’s earlier persuasive-weight position remains noncontrolling. The salary-basis construction and correction rule are separately supported by all nine Justices.

### Lynce v. Mathis, 519 U.S. 433 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** February 19, 1997.

#### Judgment

Reversed and remanded, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The district court shall determine the amount of constitutionally protected credit under the correct temporal analysis and order release if Lynce’s lawful sentence has expired.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Stevens | Stone, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer | Supports reversal and remand | Complete opinion |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Thomas | Scalia | Supports reversal and remand | Relies on the narrower ground that the State canceled credits already accrued and used |

#### Question 1: Retroactive cancellation of release credits

**Question decided:** Retroactive cancellation of release credits.

**Holding:** Florida violates the Ex Post Facto Clause when it retrospectively cancels release credits already awarded and used to release an inmate, and the cancellation lengthens actual confinement.

**Controlling explanation:** Whether a retrospective change increases punishment turns on its objective operation, not on the administrative or penological motive for originally creating the credit. A credit that determines the lawful release date is part of the effective measure of confinement.

Unlike the procedural change in *Morales*, the increase in Lynce’s punishment is neither speculative nor attenuated. Florida changed his release calculation by years and returned him to prison. Calling the credits an overcrowding device does not eliminate the punitive consequence of renewed confinement.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not protect credits never awarded or unavailable under the law governing the offense, and the exact amount attributable to materially different post-offense statutory provisions remains for remand.

**Legal basis:** Article I, § 10, Ex Post Facto Clause.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Stevens, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Morales* is distinguished and clarified. Its sufficient-risk rule remains controlling, but actual reincarceration after retroactive cancellation of accrued release credits satisfies that rule directly.

### Maryland v. Wilson, 519 U.S. 408 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** February 19, 1997.

#### Judgment

Reversed and remanded, 6-3. Supporting: O’Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Opposing: Stone, Stevens, and Kennedy.

The suppression judgment is vacated, and the Maryland courts shall proceed under the categorical passenger-exit rule.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | O’Connor | Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer | Supports reversal and remand | Complete opinion |
| Dissent | Kennedy | Stone and Stevens | Would affirm | Requires an objective circumstance connected to safety, a lawful search, or the conduct of the stop |

#### Question 1: Passenger-exit authority

**Question decided:** Passenger-exit authority.

**Holding:** During a lawful traffic stop, an officer may order passengers to exit the vehicle as a matter of course pending completion of the stop.

**Controlling explanation:** No individualized suspicion that the particular passenger is armed, dangerous, or involved in criminal activity is required for the exit order itself.

traffic stops present a weighty officer-safety interest, which may increase when multiple occupants are present. Although the passenger ordinarily committed no traffic offense, the lawful stop has already interrupted the passenger’s travel. Requiring the passenger to step outside imposes a comparatively limited additional intrusion while allowing the officer to control the immediate roadside setting.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The rule does not authorize an unlawful initial stop, a search of the passenger, detention extending beyond the lawful traffic mission, or other investigative action requiring independent justification.

**Legal basis:** Fourth Amendment.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by O’Connor, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** The decision creates the first controlling simulated rule for passenger-exit orders. *Whren* remains the rule governing the objective validity of the initial stop; *Wilson* adds categorical authority to control passenger location while that lawful stop remains in progress.

### Schenck v. Pro-Choice Network of Western New York, 519 U.S. 357 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** February 19, 1997.

#### Judgment

| Judgment component | Disposition | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Relief or remand |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed entrance and driveway zones, including the fixed-zone counseling condition | Affirmed, 6-3 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | These provisions may remain in force. |
| Person and vehicle floating zones, including the automatic 15-foot retreat outside fixed zones | Reversed, 8-1 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg | Breyer | These provisions shall be struck. |
| Narrow post-refusal disengagement provision on remand | Authorized, 6-3 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | The district court may require the enjoined parties to stop following and maintain a modest, precisely defined separation after an objectively clear refusal. |

##### Judgment, Mandate, and Remand

The judgment is affirmed in part and reversed in part. The district court may retain the fixed zones and their limited counseling exception. It shall remove the unconditional floating zones and the automatic 15-foot retreat outside the fixed zones.

A replacement provision may permit an initial peaceful approach but, after an objectively clear verbal or nonverbal refusal, require the enjoined defendants to stop following and maintain a modest, precisely defined separation supported by the record. The provision may not restrict stationary advocacy, speech addressed generally, willing conversation, or nonparties.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Stone | Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, and Ginsburg in full; Breyer as to the fixed zones, fixed-zone condition, and remand authority; Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas as to invalidation of the floating zones | Supports the mixed judgment | Different issue coalitions as stated |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Scalia | Kennedy and Thomas | Supports invalidation of floating zones; opposes the provisions left or authorized | Rejects fixed zones and listener-triggered separation |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Breyer | None | Supports fixed zones and remand authority; would affirm the floating zones | Treats the existing injunction as sufficiently tied to the local record |

#### Question 1: Fixed zones and the counseling exception

**Question decided:** Fixed zones and the counseling exception.

**Holding:** The fixed 15-foot zones around clinic doorways, driveways, and parking entrances, together with the cease-and-desist condition governing the two counselors permitted inside those zones, satisfy the First Amendment on this record.

**Controlling explanation:** The fixed geography corresponds to the places where obstruction and crowding repeatedly impaired access. The stable corridor leaves visible and audible advocacy immediately outside. The counseling condition governs only an exception that allows two speakers inside an otherwise valid clear zone; it prevents that exception from recreating the close pursuit and crowding the zone remedies.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The holding does not create a general right to avoid unwelcome speech on public sidewalks or validate a larger unsupported fixed zone.

**Legal basis:** First Amendment and the injunction-specific rule adopted in *Madsen*.

**Authority:** Stone’s opinion, joined on this issue by Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer, supplies a six-Justice majority.

#### Question 2: Floating zones

**Question decided:** Floating zones.

**Holding:** The unconditional 15-foot floating zones around persons and vehicles, and the linked automatic retreat outside the fixed zones, burden more speech than necessary.

**Controlling explanation:** A moving 15-foot boundary is uncertain in operation, prevents ordinary conversational distance and leaflet transfer, and burdens peaceful speakers far beyond the access points. Vehicle zones also restrict speakers who stand at the curb holding signs or addressing traffic without obstructing an entrance.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not foreclose direct rules against obstruction, touching, threats, trespass, or persistent pursuit.

**Authority:** Stone’s opinion is joined on this issue by Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Ginsburg, producing an eight-Justice majority.

#### Question 3: Narrow post-refusal remedy

**Question decided:** Narrow post-refusal remedy.

**Holding:** This record permits a narrower provision requiring the enjoined defendants, after an objectively clear refusal, to stop following the person addressed and maintain a modest, specifically defined separation.

**Controlling explanation:** Refusal may terminate targeted pursuit by the adjudicated parties, but it may not silence stationary advocacy, speech addressed generally, a peaceful initial approach, or willing conversation. The distance must be precisely stated and supported by the record rather than fixed automatically at 15 feet.

Direct regulation of post-refusal following addresses the proved pattern of close pursuit without converting every listener into a moving speech-restriction zone.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The holding creates no general listener’s veto or undefined entitlement to personal space.

**Authority:** Stone’s opinion, joined on this issue by Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer, supplies a six-Justice majority.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Simulated *Madsen* is applied and clarified. Fixed geographic relief may be sustained by location-specific obstruction findings. Mobile zones require separate precision and support. The decision also recognizes a narrower conduct-based remedy for persistent post-refusal pursuit by adjudicated parties, without creating a general listener’s veto.

### Brown v. Hot, Sexy & Safer Productions, Inc., 68 F.3d 525

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** February 24, 1997.

#### Judgment

Affirmed, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

Justice Kennedy delivered the Opinion of the Court, joined by every participating Justice.

#### Question 1: Parental liberty and student privacy

**Question decided:** Parental liberty and student privacy.

**Holding:** Parental liberty does not confer a constitutional right to prescribe or opt out of each public-school curricular presentation reasonably related to a legitimate pedagogical objective. Compulsory exposure to ideas, without compelled participation, affirmation, disclosure, or bodily intrusion, does not violate student privacy or substantive due process.

**Controlling explanation:** Parents retain authority to choose among lawful educational paths and to instruct their children outside school. Once a child attends public school, the Constitution does not give each parent a line-item veto over curricular content.

The students had to attend and listen, but they were not required to perform a demonstration, state agreement, disclose private information, or undergo treatment. The alleged vulgarity and the school’s possible violation of local policy may support criticism or state-law relief, but they do not identify a federal deprivation.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not approve compelled profession, personally targeted sexual conduct, bodily intrusion, religious instruction, pretextual curricular action, or sex-based humiliation.

**Legal basis:** Fourteenth Amendment.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Kennedy, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

#### Question 2: Procedural due process

**Question decided:** Procedural due process.

**Holding:** Assuming without deciding that the written positive-subscription policy created a protected state-law interest, the federal procedural claim fails because the plaintiffs did not preserve an argument that available Massachusetts postdeprivation remedies were inadequate.

**Controlling explanation:** A state policy violation is not itself a federal due-process violation. The Court does not decide whether the departure from the policy was random and unauthorized because the necessary challenge to the available state remedial process was not preserved.

**Limits and questions not reached:** State-law enforcement of the policy remains outside the granted federal questions.

**Legal basis:** Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Kennedy, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

#### Question 3: Free exercise

**Question decided:** Free exercise.

**Holding:** Compulsory attendance at the assembly does not violate free exercise when the students are not required to engage in religiously forbidden conduct, affirm the presentation’s message, or surrender a benefit because of religious objection.

**Controlling explanation:** The attendance requirement was neutral and generally applicable. Exposure to speech inconsistent with religious belief is not the same as compelled observance or conduct.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision does not govern religious targeting, compelled affirmation, or a mandatory activity itself forbidden by faith.

**Legal basis:** Free Exercise Clause.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Kennedy, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

#### Question 4: Title IX

**Question decided:** Title IX.

**Holding:** The complaint fails under Title IX because it alleges no discrimination, exclusion, or hostile educational condition imposed on the plaintiffs because of sex.

**Controlling explanation:** Sexual subject matter is not itself sex discrimination. The presentation was given to the student audience generally, and the named plaintiffs were not selected for the demonstrations. The missing because-of-sex element makes it unnecessary to decide severity or pervasiveness.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not govern sex-specific humiliation, school-authorized sexual targeting, or deliberate indifference to known sex-based harassment.

**Legal basis:** Title IX.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Kennedy, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Same-term *Curtis* is distinguished and clarified. A voluntary resource creates no burden merely by being available. *Brown* adds that mandatory attendance at a curricular presentation, without compelled affirmation, participation, disclosure, bodily intrusion, or religious conduct, likewise creates no parental line-item veto or free-exercise violation. *Settle* is applied without altering its protection for genuine curricular requirements.

### Warner-Jenkinson Co. v. Hilton Davis Chemical Co., 520 U.S. 17 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** March 3, 1997.

#### Judgment

Reversed and remanded, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The Federal Circuit shall determine the legal effect of the pH amendment. If the asserted equivalent remains legally available, disputed factual equivalence shall proceed under ordinary infringement procedures. The Court does not decide infringement finally.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Thomas | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer | Supports reversal and remand | Complete opinion |
| Concurrence | Ginsburg | Kennedy | Supports reversal and remand | Emphasizes fair notice in applying the unexplained-amendment burden |

#### Question 1: Survival and element-specific operation of equivalents

**Question decided:** Survival and element-specific operation of equivalents.

**Holding:** The doctrine of equivalents survived the 1952 Patent Act, but it must be applied to each claim element rather than to the accused product or process as a whole.

**Controlling explanation:** Nonliteral infringement may be found only when each claimed element is present literally or through a legally permissible equivalent. The doctrine may not erase or vitiate a material claim limitation.

The doctrine prevents trivial substitutions from defeating a lawful patent, while element-specific application preserves the statutory claim’s notice and boundary functions. The 1952 Act did not clearly displace the doctrine recognized in *Graver Tank*.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court adopts no single verbal formula for equivalence and leaves case-specific refinement to the Federal Circuit.

**Legal basis:** Patent Act of 1952 and surviving patent precedent.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Thomas, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

#### Question 2: Prosecution-history estoppel and unexplained amendments

**Question decided:** Prosecution-history estoppel and unexplained amendments.

**Holding:** Subject matter surrendered during patent prosecution may not be recaptured through equivalents. When the record does not disclose why a narrowing amendment was made, the patentee bears the burden of establishing a reason that does not estop the asserted equivalent.

**Controlling explanation:** The court determines the legal availability of the asserted equivalent under the claim and prosecution history. If the patentee cannot supply a nonestopping explanation for an unexplained narrowing amendment, the disputed territory is presumed surrendered.

The public is entitled to rely on the claim and the prosecution record. The upper pH limit was added to distinguish prior art, but the reason for the lower 6.0 limit is unresolved. The existing infringement judgment therefore cannot stand without determining the legal effect of that amendment.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision creates no categorical bar for every foreseeable but unclaimed substitute absent a narrowing amendment. It does not decide a broader intent-based theory or remove disputed factual equivalence from the jury after the court resolves the legal limits.

**Legal basis:** Patent Act, claim construction, and prosecution-history estoppel.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Thomas, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Markman v. Westview Instruments* is applied without alteration. Courts decide claim meaning and the legal effect of prosecution history; genuine factual equivalence remains subject to ordinary infringement procedures when the asserted equivalent survives those legal limits.

### Wright v. MetroHealth Medical Center, 58 F.3d 1130

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** March 3, 1997.

#### Judgment

Affirmed, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The federal constitutional judgment remains in force. The Court makes no separate ruling on the merits of the pendent state-law theories.

Justice Kennedy delivered the Opinion of the Court, joined by every participating Justice.

#### Question 1: Anti-nepotism policy and the right to marry

**Question decided:** Anti-nepotism policy and the right to marry.

**Holding:** A public employer does not directly and substantially interfere with marriage when it requires one spouse to leave a work unit in which the spouses necessarily interact, provides its employee a comparable transfer without loss of pay, and neither prohibits the marriage nor conditions continued marital status on loss of public employment.

**Controlling explanation:** The policy regulates simultaneous assignment within one operational unit, not eligibility to marry or remain married. The Wrights married despite the policy, and Martha remained eligible for comparable employment throughout MetroHealth’s system. The burden is real but indirect, of the kind that *Jobst* distinguished from the legal and practical barriers invalidated in *Loving* and *Zablocki*.

Under rational-basis review, MetroHealth may address actual and perceived conflicts of interest, divided loyalty, crew coordination, and confidence in assignment and safety decisions within a small emergency-flight team. It need not prove that every married pair will compromise operations. Applying the rule only where family members work in close and recurring proximity is rational line drawing, not evidence that the policy is arbitrary.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision does not approve a policy intended to deter marriage, automatic discharge of one spouse, sex-based administration, enforcement resting on animus, or a transfer materially inferior in pay or responsibility. It does not decide a completed discharge claim because no such discharge occurred.

**Legal basis:** Fourteenth Amendment Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Kennedy, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** The received distinction between direct legal impediments to marriage and incidental economic or employment consequences is applied without alteration. The decision supplies the first controlling simulated application of that distinction to a public-employer anti-nepotism policy.

---

### Brown v. Polk County, 61 F.3d 650

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** March 17, 1997.

#### Judgment

| Judgment component | Disposition | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Relief or remand |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Religion-specific workplace directives and removal order | Affirmed, 9-0 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | None | The directives may not be enforced as blanket prohibitions. The remand may preserve neutral and tailored workplace rules. |
| Title VII religious-discrimination judgment concerning discharge | Affirmed, 6-3 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | The remand for appropriate statutory relief continues; the County may not reopen the completed trial record to supply a same-decision defense it failed to prove. |

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | O’Connor | Stone, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer in full; Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas as to accommodation boundaries and the First Amendment judgment | Supports affirmance | Complete opinion for six Justices; partial joins as stated |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Kennedy | Scalia and Thomas | Supports the First Amendment judgment but opposes final resolution of the same-decision defense | Would remand the mixed-motive question for district-court findings |

#### Question 1: Title VII accommodation and public resources

**Question decided:** Title VII accommodation and public resources.

**Holding:** Title VII requires reasonable accommodation of a known sincere religious practice unless the employer establishes a real, more-than-de-minimis operational burden. It does not require diversion of public employees or resources to private religious work, official worship through supervisory authority, coercive religious counseling, harassment, or unequal personal use of the workplace.

**Controlling explanation:** Genuinely voluntary employee-initiated prayer, private religious conversation, and personal religious items must be distinguished from expression attributable to the government or dependent on public resources. Generalized discomfort, offense, speculative polarization, and unsupported fear of favoritism do not establish undue hardship.

**Application:** Polk County could prevent Brown from directing a secretary to prepare Bible-study notes. It could also regulate prayer or religious instruction delivered as an official supervisory act. The record did not establish a real operational burden from every private conversation, voluntary prayer, or personal religious item swept into the County’s categorical orders.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Comparable secular personal use may be restricted through a neutral rule. Title VII does not authorize favoritism, compulsory prayer, harassment, or religious use of subordinates.

**Legal basis:** Title VII, 42 U.S.C. §§ 2000e(j) and 2000e-2.

**Authority:** O’Connor’s opinion is joined on these accommodation propositions by all nine Justices.

#### Question 2: Religion as a factor in discharge

**Question decided:** Religion as a factor in discharge.

**Holding:** Under the law governing the pre-1991 conduct, Brown produced direct evidence that religion was a motivating factor in his discharge, and Polk County failed on the completed trial record to prove that it would have made the same decision without considering the protected religious practices.

**Controlling explanation:** The administrator testified that the religion-based reprimand was a factor in the discharge. That admission activated the received mixed-motive framework. The County had a full trial at which to establish its asserted budgetary and supervisory grounds, but its decisionmaker could not say that Brown would have been discharged absent the religious factor, and the record supplied no other proof carrying the County’s burden. A second evidentiary opportunity is not required merely because the district court initially applied the wrong framework.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The holding does not prevent discharge for independently established poor performance, misuse of public resources, or coercive supervision. It does not apply the Civil Rights Act of 1991 retroactively.

**Legal basis:** Title VII and the pre-1991 mixed-motive rule.

**Authority:** O’Connor’s opinion, joined on this question by Stone, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer, supplies a six-Justice majority.

#### Question 3: Religion-specific directives and attribution

**Question decided:** Religion-specific directives and attribution.

**Holding:** A public employer violates the First Amendment when it singles out religious exercise and viewpoint through an undifferentiated prohibition on everything that could be considered witnessing, counseling, or proselytizing and orders removal of every religious item without tying those restrictions to official duties, coercion, harassment, resource use, or demonstrated disruption.

**Controlling explanation:** Government may control speech and worship delivered as its own, restrict coercive supervision, and enforce neutral rules governing time, duties, resources, and workplace conduct. It may not treat the religious character of otherwise private expression as the workplace harm.

The directives reached far beyond the activities that could lawfully be regulated. They covered a personal Bible kept in a desk, private conversation, and any expression someone might characterize as religious. Avoiding an objectively grounded Establishment Clause violation is a legitimate public-employer interest, especially where a supervisor leads worship in a mandatory meeting. Abstract fear of establishment or offense does not justify suppressing private religious expression.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision does not require identical treatment of government-sponsored worship and private employee expression, or make a statutory accommodation violation automatically establish a constitutional violation.

**Legal basis:** Free Speech and Free Exercise Clauses, informed by the Establishment Clause’s attribution boundary.

**Authority:** Unanimous.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Beadle v. City of Tampa* is applied and clarified. Its real-burden requirement governs private religious practices, while public resource use, official worship, coercion, and harassment remain independently regulable. *Waters*, *National Treasury Employees Union*, *Pinette*, and *Chabad-Lubavitch* are applied through the distinction between private expression and speech attributable to government.

### Young v. Harper, 520 U.S. 143 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** March 18, 1997.

#### Judgment

Affirmed, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

Oklahoma may continue Harper’s custody only through a lawful revocation determination or another independent legal basis. The Court does not order unconditional release.

Justice Thomas delivered the Opinion of the Court, joined by every participating Justice.

#### Question 1: Parole-like community release

**Question decided:** Parole-like community release.

**Holding:** A State must provide the procedures required by *Morrissey* before terminating a conditional-release program that releases a prisoner from the institution to live and work in the community under restrictions materially equivalent to parole.

**Controlling explanation:** Legal labels do not control. The inquiry concerns the liberty actually conferred, including residence outside the institution, employment, ordinary community life, and supervision resembling parole. The rule does not create an entitlement to initial release.

Harper maintained his own residence and employment and lived generally free of the incidents of imprisonment. Reporting, travel, and behavioral conditions did not make that community liberty institutional confinement. Oklahoma could treat the Governor’s denial of parole as relevant to whether preparole should continue, but it could not extinguish the liberty already conferred without notice, an opportunity to contest the asserted basis for return, and a neutral decision under the appropriate revocation procedures.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision does not govern short furloughs, work details, or release arrangements that remain functionally institutional. Immediate temporary custody remains possible in a genuine safety emergency if prompt effective process follows.

**Legal basis:** Fourteenth Amendment Due Process Clause.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Thomas, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Morrissey* is applied and clarified. Its protections extend to a release program equivalent to parole in operation, notwithstanding a different program label. Simulated *Sandin* remains confined to claimed liberty interests within institutional confinement.

### Lambert v. Wicklund, 520 U.S. 292 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** March 31, 1997.

#### Judgment

Reversed and remanded, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The injunction is vacated insofar as it rests on the asserted defect in the best-interests formulation. Any preserved issue not resolved by this judgment remains for further proceedings.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Per curiam Opinion of the Court | The Court | Stone, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, and Thomas | Supports reversal and remand | Complete opinion |
| Concurrence in the judgment | Stevens | Ginsburg and Breyer | Supports reversal and remand | Agrees the Montana route is constitutionally sufficient while reserving whether an abortion-best-interests finding is also necessary |

#### Question 1: Best-interests bypass for parental notification

**Question decided:** Best-interests bypass for parental notification.

**Holding:** A confidential and expeditious judicial bypass satisfies the best-interests component of the parental-notification rule when it requires waiver upon a finding that notifying the parent is not in the minor’s best interests.

**Controlling explanation:** Constitutional sufficiency turns on whether the decisionmaker can authorize the abortion without notice when parental involvement would be contrary to the minor’s interests, not on use of a particular verbal formula.

Montana’s language is materially equivalent to the Ohio formulation previously sustained. Read in context, a finding that notification is not in the minor’s best interests directs the court to authorize abortion without notification. The maturity route, confidentiality, appointed counsel, deadline, and automatic-waiver provision reinforce the availability of effective independent review. The Ninth Circuit could not facially invalidate the statute by separating two formulations that produce the same legal authorization.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not decide the validity of clear-and-convincing proof in every application, the adequacy of the emergency provisions, or whether implementation could make the nominally expedited process unavailable.

**Legal basis:** Fourteenth Amendment.

**Authority:** The six-Justice per curiam opinion supplies the controlling rationale. All nine Justices agree that the statutory best-interests route is constitutionally sufficient.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Simulated *Planned Parenthood v. Miller* is applied and clarified. Its best-interests requirement concerns effective authority to dispense with notice, not a mandatory phrasing of the judicial inquiry.

### Robinson v. City of Edmond, 68 F.3d 1226

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** March 31, 1997.

#### Judgment

| Judgment component | Disposition | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Relief or remand |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Article III standing | Standing sustained, 7-2 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Scalia, Thomas | The Court reaches the municipal Establishment Clause claim. |
| Establishment Clause judgment | Affirmed, 6-3 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | Edmond shall cease using the cross-bearing seal as its official imprimatur within a reasonable implementation period set on remand. |

The district court may permit archival preservation and genuinely historical displays with accurate contextual treatment. Individual damages and immunity remain separate from the municipal prospective relief.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | O’Connor | Stone, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer in full; Kennedy as to standing | Supports affirmance | Complete opinion for six Justices; standing portion joined by seven |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Kennedy | None | Supports standing but would reverse on the merits | Would require coercion, legal preference, or another more concrete governmental religious disability |
| Dissent | Scalia | Thomas | Would dismiss for lack of standing and, alternatively, reverse on the merits | Rejects direct-exposure standing and treats the seal as permissible historical civic symbolism |

#### Question 1: Standing to challenge the official seal

**Question decided:** Standing to challenge the official seal.

**Holding:** Residents and workers who are regularly confronted with a municipality’s own official seal in ordinary civic transactions suffer a direct and continuing injury sufficient to seek prospective relief from the seal’s allegedly unconstitutional governmental message.

**Controlling explanation:** Mere knowledge that government has engaged in disputed conduct, or abstract ideological disagreement by a person lacking direct contact, remains insufficient. Regular exposure to the government’s own official identifier through bills, uniforms, vehicles, signs, and civic proceedings is not the remote observation rejected in *Valley Forge*.

The plaintiffs live or work under a municipal government that repeatedly presents the challenged seal as its authenticating mark. Their asserted injury therefore arises from direct recurring governmental communication, not simply from awareness of conduct occurring elsewhere.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not create standing whenever a person learns of an allegedly unconstitutional symbol or disagrees with a historical display encountered only by choice.

**Legal basis:** Article III.

**Authority:** O’Connor’s opinion, joined on standing by Stone, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer, supplies a seven-Justice majority.

#### Question 2: Christian cross in the official city seal

**Question decided:** Christian cross in the official city seal.

**Holding:** A municipality violates the Establishment Clause when it incorporates an unmistakable Christian cross into its official seal and uses that seal pervasively as the government’s own identifying and authenticating mark.

**Controlling explanation:** Attribution, governmental authorship, control, placement, and use determine the constitutional character of the message. Secular images elsewhere in a seal and a historical explanation do not neutralize a sectarian symbol that the government presents as part of its official self-description.

Edmond selected and owns the seal, controls every official use, and places it on the instruments through which the City speaks and acts. The cross therefore is not the message of a private speaker in an open forum. Its placement among the City’s chosen civic emblems identifies Christianity as part of the government’s official identity. The engine, oil derrick, tower, and covered wagon do not transform the cross into a religiously neutral graphic, and longevity does not cure governmental adoption of a faith’s unmistakable symbol.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The holding does not invalidate the City’s name, private religious displays in neutral forums, archival retention, a contextual historical exhibit, or ceremonial references that do not adopt a religion as the government’s own.

**Legal basis:** Establishment Clause.

**Authority:** O’Connor’s opinion, joined on the merits by Stone, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer, supplies a six-Justice majority.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Capitol Square v. Pinette* and *Chabad-Lubavitch* are distinguished. Their attribution rules protect private religious expression in neutral forums; they do not insulate a religious symbol chosen and pervasively used by government as its own official mark. The decision supplies the first controlling simulated rule for a sectarian symbol incorporated into a municipal seal.

### Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. v. Federal Communications Commission, 520 U.S. 180 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** March 31, 1997.

#### Judgment

Affirmed, 5-4. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, and Breyer. Opposing: O’Connor, Scalia, Thomas, and Ginsburg.

The must-carry provisions remain in force. Properly supported system-specific as-applied challenges remain available.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion announcing the judgment and Opinion of the Court except in part | Kennedy | Stone, Stevens, and Souter in full; Breyer except insofar as the opinion relies on an anticompetitive rationale | Supports affirmance | Court opinion on preservation of free local broadcasting, multiplicity of sources, record support, burden, and fit |
| Concurrence | Stevens | None | Supports affirmance | Emphasizes the legitimacy of Congress’s supported judgment concerning the communications structure |
| Concurrence in part | Breyer | None | Supports affirmance | Relies on preserving free local broadcasting and a multiplicity of information sources, not the anticompetitive rationale |
| Dissent | O’Connor | Scalia, Thomas, and Ginsburg | Would reverse | Rejects the record showing and maintains the classification and editorial-discretion objections stated in simulated *Turner I* |

#### Question 1: Record support for the governmental interests

**Question decided:** Record support for the governmental interests.

**Holding:** The expanded record supports Congress’s reasonable predictive judgment that, without must-carry, cable bottleneck control would threaten carriage and economic viability of local broadcast stations, thereby impairing free over-the-air service and the dissemination of information from multiple sources.

**Controlling explanation:** Congress could rely on evidence of growing cable market power, vertical integration, incentives to drop or disadvantage unaffiliated broadcasters, prior noncarriage, and the relationship among carriage, audience reach, advertising revenue, and continued broadcast operation. Intermediate scrutiny does not require proof that the entire broadcasting industry would collapse or that every individual station faced imminent failure. Courts independently review constitutional fit while according proper weight to legislative predictions supported by substantial evidence.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not apply broadcast-scarcity doctrine to cable or treat legislative assertion without supporting evidence as conclusive.

**Authority:** Kennedy’s opinion is joined on the free-broadcasting and multiplicity rationales by Stone, Stevens, Souter, and Breyer, supplying a five-Justice majority. The additional anticompetitive rationale is supported by Kennedy, Stone, Stevens, and Souter only and is not independently controlling.

#### Question 2: Editorial burden and fit

**Question decided:** Editorial burden and fit.

**Holding:** The must-carry provisions do not burden substantially more cable editorial discretion than necessary to advance the majority-supported interests.

**Controlling explanation:** The obligations are limited by system capacity, count qualifying stations already carried voluntarily, and leave operators control over the substantial remainder of their lineups. The developed evidence showed that most systems used otherwise available capacity and that relatively few existing cable services were displaced. Congress was not required to select a less effective alternative merely because one could be imagined; intermediate scrutiny requires reasonable fit, not least-restrictive-means proof.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision does not immunize a materially more burdensome future rule or foreclose an as-applied challenge supported by disproportionate actual displacement.

**Legal basis:** First Amendment and 47 U.S.C. §§ 534 and 535.

**Authority:** Kennedy’s opinion, joined on this question by Stone, Stevens, Souter, and Breyer, supplies a five-Justice majority.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Simulated *Turner I* is applied and completed. Its content-neutral classification, intermediate-scrutiny standard, burden allocation, and allowance for supported legislative prediction remain unchanged. The evidentiary gap that required the 1994 remand is now closed.

### Young v. Fordice, 520 U.S. 273 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** March 31, 1997.

#### Judgment

Reversed and remanded, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The District Court shall identify Mississippi’s covered discretionary changes and enjoin their further administration as appropriate unless and until they receive § 5 preclearance. It shall not decide discriminatory purpose, retrogression, or entitlement to preclearance.

Justice Breyer delivered the Opinion of the Court, joined by every participating Justice.

#### Question 1: The operative baseline

**Question decided:** The operative baseline.

**Holding:** The Provisional Plan did not become the voting practice in force or effect for purposes of the § 5 comparison baseline.

**Controlling explanation:** Unlawfulness under state law alone would not prevent a longstanding actual practice from becoming the baseline. Here, however, officials expected the plan to become lawful, abandoned it promptly when the legislature failed to act, used it for only forty-one days, obtained implementation by only about one-third of registration officials, and conducted no election under it. Taken together, those circumstances show a temporary and incomplete attempt rather than a settled operative system. The Old System therefore remains the baseline.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not establish a fixed duration or numerical threshold for determining when a practice becomes operative.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Breyer, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

#### Question 2: Discretionary NVRA implementation changes

**Question decided:** Discretionary NVRA implementation changes.

**Holding:** Discretionary state choices used to implement the NVRA are changes requiring § 5 preclearance when they differ from the lawful baseline, even though the State made them while complying with federal law.

**Controlling explanation:** Federal or superior legal constraints do not preclear the policy choices left to state or local officials. Change triggers the preclearance sequence regardless of whether its eventual effect is beneficial, harmful, or neutral. The enforcement court identifies coverage and requires nonuse; the designated preclearance forums decide purpose and effect.

**Application:** Mississippi adopted materially different registration instructions, assistance practices, agency designations, reporting rules, forwarding procedures, forms, and communications. Those choices could affect who registers, what applicants understand, and how officials administer federal and state voting eligibility. They therefore require preclearance. Mississippi’s earlier submission described a materially different unitary system and did not clearly submit the later dual system.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not decide whether separate federal and state rolls are substantively lawful or whether the identified changes should receive preclearance. The judgment addresses discretionary state implementation. It does not decide whether direct compliance with an express federal command that leaves no state policy choice is itself a state voting change. Same-term *Lopez* remains controlling for changes mandated by a noncovered State.

**Legal basis:** Voting Rights Act § 5 and the National Voter Registration Act’s non-displacement provisions.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Breyer, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Same-term *Lopez v. Monterey County* is applied and clarified. Its rejection of a general no-discretion exemption remains controlling for state-mandated changes. *Young v. Fordice* adds that federal compliance does not remove discretionary state policy choices from § 5 and identifies the circumstances under which a brief provisional practice fails to replace the prior baseline.

### Chandler v. Miller, 520 U.S. 305 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** April 15, 1997.

#### Judgment

Reversed and remanded, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The District Court shall enter declaratory and prospective relief barring enforcement of the drug-test qualification. Georgia remains free to investigate particularized wrongdoing and impose lawful nonsearch qualifications.

Justice Ginsburg delivered the Opinion of the Court, joined by every participating Justice.

#### Question 1: Suspicionless testing of candidates

**Question decided:** Suspicionless testing of candidates.

**Holding:** A State may not require every candidate for designated public office to undergo suspicionless drug testing when it identifies no substantial and concrete special need connected to the actual duties or risks of the covered offices.

**Controlling explanation:** Reduced intrusiveness cannot substitute for the threshold governmental need. A departure from individualized suspicion requires a substantial operational concern beyond ordinary law enforcement or symbolic reassurance, followed by a context-specific assessment of privacy, efficacy, and fit.

The covered offices share no common immediate safety risk, candidates remain private citizens unless elected, and public candidacy does not waive bodily privacy. Georgia demonstrated no drug crisis among officeholders and no reason ordinary investigation of particularized misconduct would be impracticable. The candidate-selected testing date also makes the program poorly suited to identify or deter drug use. The State’s remaining interest is a symbolic display of commitment to drug control, and symbolic reassurance is not a special need.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision does not govern targeted testing based on individualized suspicion, medical fitness examinations, financial-disclosure rules, private-sector testing, or security screening tied to a real and immediate safety risk.

**Legal basis:** Fourth Amendment.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Ginsburg, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Simulated *Vernonia* is declined extension beyond its documented school-athletics setting. The decision clarifies that a minimally intrusive procedure does not independently justify suspicionless testing when the asserted special need is missing.

---

### Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** April 21, 1997.

#### Judgment

Vacated and remanded, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The lower courts shall require the plaintiffs to identify each specific statutory right asserted. Only after deciding whether a particular provision creates an individual right may the court address § 1983 displacement, proper defendants, causation, and lawful relief. No undifferentiated order of programwide substantial compliance may issue.

#### Opinions

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | O’Connor | Stone, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer | Supports vacatur and remand | Complete opinion |
| Concurrence | Scalia | Kennedy | Supports vacatur and remand | Questions whether Spending Clause beneficiaries may sue as third-party beneficiaries under § 1983, while accepting the governing *Wright* and *Wilder* framework for this case |

#### Question 1: Identification of enforceable Title IV-D rights

**Question decided:** Identification of enforceable Title IV-D rights.

**Holding:** Title IV-D does not create an individual federal right to compel a State to achieve systemwide substantial compliance with the title as a whole.

**Controlling explanation:** A § 1983 claimant must identify a particular statutory provision intended to benefit the claimant, imposing a binding obligation, and defining an interest sufficiently concrete for judicial enforcement. The inquiry proceeds provision by provision. Aggregate program standards, staffing requirements, data systems, service duties, and payment-distribution commands cannot be treated as one indivisible entitlement.

Title IV-D’s substantial-compliance yardstick measures aggregate state performance for federal audit and funding purposes and tolerates nonperformance in some individual cases. It therefore does not promise each eligible family that the entire program will satisfy every statutory and regulatory requirement. Staffing and organizational provisions likewise do not define a manageable individual entitlement. A more specific payment-distribution or service provision may perform different legal work and must be considered separately.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court does not foreclose a claim under a specific rights-creating provision or determine whether the prior version of § 657 creates a concrete right to prompt distribution of collected payments.

**Legal basis:** 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and Title IV-D.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by O’Connor, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

#### Question 2: Statutory displacement of § 1983

**Question decided:** Statutory displacement of § 1983.

**Holding:** Title IV-D’s general audit, corrective-action, and funding-reduction mechanisms do not categorically foreclose § 1983 actions to enforce every concrete individual right the statute may create.

**Controlling explanation:** After a right is identified, § 1983 remains presumptively available unless Congress expressly foreclosed it or established a remedial scheme so comprehensive and incompatible that individual enforcement cannot coexist with the statutory design.

The Secretary’s oversight powers regulate the federal-state funding relationship but provide no general judicial or administrative forum in which an individual family may obtain case-specific relief. That mechanism is materially less comprehensive than the remedial schemes previously found to displace § 1983.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The holding creates no statutory right, authorizes no structural remedy, and does not prevent a specific remedial provision from displacing § 1983 for a particular claim.

**Legal basis:** 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and Title IV-D’s enforcement provisions.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by O’Connor, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Livadas v. Bradshaw* is applied and clarified. A complex federal funding statute must be parsed provision by provision, and categorical § 1983 displacement cannot be established merely by pointing to aggregate federal oversight and funding sanctions.

### New Mexico Department of Human Services v. Joseph A. and Josephine A., 69 F.3d 1081

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** April 21, 1997.

#### Judgment

Affirmed, 9-0. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer.

The Tenth Circuit’s remand remains in force. The District Court shall retain the decree while making adequate findings on the existing record or conducting lawful additional proceedings. It shall terminate the decree when the Department establishes the agreed twelve-month condition under the correct standard.

Justice Kennedy delivered the Opinion of the Court, joined by every participating Justice.

#### Question 1: Substantial compliance and Rule 52 findings

**Question decided:** Substantial compliance and Rule 52 findings.

**Holding:** This institutional consent decree may be dissolved only on reviewable findings that the Department maintained substantial and continuous compliance with the decree’s essential purposes for twelve consecutive months. Findings that state ultimate conclusions without explaining material deviations, methodology, and supporting subsidiary facts do not satisfy Rule 52(a).

**Controlling explanation:** Substantial compliance does not require perfection or literal satisfaction of every numerical criterion. It requires performance equivalent to compliance with the decree’s essential purposes, with only immaterial deviations. The court must identify the governing obligation, explain whether departures from specified criteria materially impair the decree’s objectives, state how it evaluated quantitative and qualitative evidence, and make enough subsidiary findings to permit meaningful appellate review.

The decree’s central purposes include fair, reasonable, and timely decisionmaking and durable procedures for permanent placement. The report acknowledged serious shortfalls and cases in which children remained in temporary care, yet often declared substantial compliance without explaining why the deviations were immaterial. It discounted adverse case studies without showing that they were aberrational, failed to resolve challenges to the reliability of the principal data system, and did not disclose a methodology permitting review. Appellate judges may not reconstruct those missing findings from a voluminous record.

**Application:** The termination order was properly vacated. The District Court must apply the decree’s text and the stated findings rule, but this Court makes no finding whether New Mexico ultimately complied.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The decision does not require perfect compliance, make every numerical target indispensable, permit expansion of the decree beyond its terms, or authorize federal control after the termination condition has been established. Termination is neither a reward nor a sanction; it follows from proof of the condition written into the federal judgment.

**Legal basis:** Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 52(a) and 53, the consent decree, and federal equitable authority over judgments.

**Authority:** Opinion of the Court by Kennedy, joined as stated in the Judgment and Opinions above; the proposition is controlling at the stated scope.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Missouri v. Jenkins* is applied without alteration. Its violation-remedy nexus and withdrawal principles do not replace a consent decree’s own termination clause. The present decision adds a decree-specific Rule 52 requirement for reviewable findings before systemic relief is dissolved.
