### College Savings Bank v. Florida Prepaid Postsecondary Education Expense Board, 527 U.S. 666 (1999)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** June 23, 1999.

**Judgment:** Affirmed in part, vacated in part, reversed in part, and remanded; votes vary by component.

| Docket or judgment component | Supreme Court disposition | Supporting Justices | Opposing Justices | Remedy or remand |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Constructive waiver as a basis for monetary relief | Affirmed, 9-0 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer | No Justice | Florida Prepaid’s participation in interstate commerce does not establish consent to suit. |
| Retrospective compensatory Lanham Act claim | Vacated and remanded, 7-2 | Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | Scalia, Thomas | The dismissal is vacated for application of the commercial-state-enterprise and remedial-autonomy rules. |
| Prospective Lanham Act claim | Reversed and remanded, 5-4 | Stone, Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer | O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | The prospective claim shall proceed subject to standing, recurrence, statutory merits, causation, and equitable-remedy requirements. |

**Remedy or remand:** The judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit is affirmed insofar as it rejects constructive waiver, vacated as to retrospective compensatory relief, and reversed as to the prospective claim. On remand, the lower courts shall determine whether Florida Prepaid satisfies the commercial-state-enterprise test and, if it does not, whether Florida provides an adequate state compensatory forum. The prospective claim shall be adjudicated on its ordinary constitutional, statutory, and equitable requirements.

**Opinions:**

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Stone | Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer as to Question 1; O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg as to Questions 2 and 3; Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, Breyer as to Question 4 | Supports the judgment at the stated issue-specific scopes | Scope stated by question |
| Concurrence in part and in the judgment | Stevens | Breyer | Supports vacatur and remand of the monetary claim and reversal and remand of the prospective claim | Joins Questions 1 and 4; would permit Congress to authorize the federal compensatory action under Article I without a commercial-enterprise inquiry or state-forum option |
| Concurrence in part and dissent in part | Scalia | Thomas | Supports the constructive-waiver holding; opposes the remaining dispositions | Joins Question 1; would retain categorical immunity from the private Article I monetary claim and would reject the direct-State prospective action |
| Dissent in part | O’Connor | Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas | Would affirm dismissal of the prospective claim | Question 4 only |

#### Question 1: Constructive waiver through commercial activity

**Question decided:** Whether a State waives sovereign immunity merely by participating in federally regulated interstate commerce after Congress announces that private suit will follow.

**Holding:** A State does not waive sovereign immunity merely by engaging in interstate commercial activity after Congress announces that private suit will follow. Waiver requires an unequivocal and voluntary manifestation of the State’s own consent. Commercial activity determines regulatory coverage and may bear on the separate commercial-state-enterprise rule, but it does not fictionally constitute consent.

**Authority:** Stone’s Opinion of the Court is joined on this proposition by Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer and is controlling.

**Controlling explanation:** Waiver concerns the State’s voluntary legal act, not Congress’s description of the consequences of regulated conduct. Florida enacted no consent, voluntarily invoked no federal forum, accepted no separately valid funding condition carrying clear notice of suit, and made no litigation commitment. Its decision to market a tuition program therefore does not communicate consent. Express consent, voluntary invocation of federal jurisdiction, and acceptance of a separately valid condition remain distinct routes.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Parden v. Terminal Railway* is overruled to the extent it recognizes constructive waiver from ordinary participation in federally regulated commerce. Its result may not be recast as consent; any liability of a state commercial enterprise must rest on the distinct substantive rule stated in Question 2.

#### Question 2: Commercial state enterprises in interstate markets

**Question decided:** Whether Congress may subject a state-owned enterprise operating voluntarily in an interstate commercial market to the ordinary compensatory remedies governing private competitors in that market.

**Holding:** When Congress unmistakably regulates an interstate commercial market, it may subject a state-owned enterprise to the ordinary compensatory remedies governing that market if the enterprise voluntarily engages in commercial sales or services in competition with private actors and possesses sufficient operational and fiscal separation that liability runs primarily against enterprise revenues or assets rather than operating as an ordinary charge on the State’s general governmental treasury.

**Authority:** Stone’s Opinion of the Court, joined on this proposition by O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg, supplies a five-Justice majority. Stevens and Breyer concur in the judgment on the broader ground that clearly authorized Article I compensation may proceed without this classification. Scalia and Thomas would retain categorical immunity.

**Controlling explanation:** The inquiry considers the enterprise’s separate legal identity; ownership and control of operating revenues; responsibility for debts and judgments; commercial sales, licensing, and contracting; competition with private firms; capacity to sue and contract; the source from which a judgment will be paid; the degree of direct state control; and whether the challenged conduct is commercial rather than an exercise of regulatory, taxing, enforcement, or other coercive sovereign authority. No single label or factor is conclusive. The required separation exists only when ordinary compensatory liability is borne primarily by the enterprise and its market revenues or assets rather than by the general governmental treasury.

**Application:** The record establishes that Florida Prepaid marketed a tuition program in competition with private providers, but it does not supply sufficient findings concerning Florida Prepaid’s legal identity, control of revenues, responsibility for debts and judgments, source of payment, or operational independence. The lower courts must decide the commercial-state-enterprise question on remand.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Commercial participation is not waiver and does not by itself establish that an entity is outside the State for arm-of-State purposes. The rule requires unmistakable federal regulation of the interstate market, voluntary commercial competition, and sufficient operational and fiscal separation. It does not subject a State’s regulatory, taxing, enforcement, or other coercive sovereign activity to ordinary market remedies, and it does not decide punitive or exemplary relief.

#### Question 3: Compensatory claim when the entity does not satisfy the commercial-enterprise rule

**Question decided:** What remedial route governs the clearly authorized federal compensatory claim if Florida Prepaid does not satisfy the commercial-state-enterprise test.

**Holding:** If Florida Prepaid does not satisfy the commercial-state-enterprise rule, Florida may require College Savings to pursue an adequate state compensation procedure for the federal Lanham Act obligation. If Florida supplies no constitutionally and practically adequate substitute forum or remedy, the clearly authorized federal compensatory action may proceed.

**Authority:** Stone’s Opinion of the Court, joined on this proposition by O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg, supplies a five-Justice majority. Stevens and Breyer concur in the judgment on the broader ground that the federal compensatory action may proceed without a state-forum option. Scalia and Thomas reject the Article I monetary route.

**Controlling explanation:** State sovereign immunity permits control over the initial forum and remedial machinery for a retrospective treasury claim, but not extinction of the substantive federal obligation. An adequate substitute must provide a neutral adjudicator, reasonable access and timeliness, authority to award substantially the full compensatory entitlement, and an enforceable payment obligation. A nominal, discretionary, discriminatorily unavailable, or practically incapable remedy is not adequate.

**Application:** The Trademark Remedy Clarification Act unmistakably identifies States and supplies the ordinary compensatory remedies for the regulated interstate market. The existing record does not establish whether Florida provides an adequate compensatory forum for the alleged Lanham Act injury. If an adequate forum exists, Florida may require its use. If none exists, the federal compensatory claim may proceed.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Competitive injury caused by a rival’s statements about its own product is not, without appropriation, destruction, or exclusionary control of protected property, an independent Fourteenth Amendment deprivation. That conclusion forecloses the asserted § 5 route but does not determine the Article I routes stated in Questions 2 and 3. Falsity, materiality, injury, causation, the amount of compensation, and any enhanced or punitive relief remain unresolved.

#### Question 4: Expressly authorized prospective relief

**Question decided:** Whether the Trademark Remedy Clarification Act validly authorizes prospective Lanham Act relief directly against a State.

**Holding:** The Trademark Remedy Clarification Act validly authorizes a prospective Lanham Act action directly against a State when the plaintiff establishes an ongoing or imminently threatened statutory violation and satisfies ordinary Article III and equitable-remedy requirements.

**Authority:** Stone’s Opinion of the Court, joined on this proposition by Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer, supplies a five-Justice majority.

**Controlling explanation:** Congress acted within its commerce authority, unmistakably identified States as defendants, created the cause of action, and supplied the prospective remedy. This route does not depend on waiver, commercial-enterprise status, or the availability of a state compensatory forum. The present record does not conclusively establish that the challenged representations continued or were likely to recur when relief would issue.

**Application:** On remand, College Savings must prove injury, recurrence or imminent threat, falsity, materiality, causation, and entitlement to a properly confined injunction or declaration.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Hess v. Port Authority Trans-Hudson Corp.* is applied and clarified. Arm-of-State status turns on legal and fiscal reality, while the commercial-state-enterprise rule separately determines the remedial consequences of voluntary market operation by an entity that is otherwise treated as the State. *SSC Corp. v. Town of Smithtown* is applied by analogy to distinguish voluntary purchasing and commercial market participation from coercive regulation of outsiders; its dormant Commerce Clause holding remains unchanged. *Seminole Tribe v. Florida* is clarified; that decision sustained an unmistakably enacted prospective Article I action and reserved retrospective compensatory relief. *City of Boerne v. Flores* is applied; the competitive injury alleged here is not an independent Fourteenth Amendment property deprivation, but that conclusion does not foreclose relief resting on a valid Article I route. *Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife* is applied; prospective relief requires concrete injury, ongoing or imminent recurrence, causation, and redressability.

### Alden v. Maine, 527 U.S. 706 (1999)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** June 23, 1999.

**Judgment:** Vacated and remanded, 7-2. Supporting: Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Opposing: Scalia and Thomas.

**Remedy or remand:** The judgment of the Supreme Judicial Court of Maine is vacated. The case is remanded for determination of whether Maine supplies an adequate remedial system capable of enforcing the federal wage entitlement. If Maine supplies such a system, it may require the probation officers to use it. If Maine supplies no adequate substitute, a Maine court possessing ordinary jurisdiction over comparable claims must hear the FLSA action.

**Opinions:**

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Stone | O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg | Supports vacatur and remand | Complete opinion |
| Concurrence in the judgment | Stevens | Breyer | Supports vacatur and remand | Would permit Congress to authorize the FLSA action directly without a state-forum option |
| Dissent | Scalia | Thomas | Would affirm | Would retain categorical state immunity from the private Article I monetary action |

#### Question 1: Article I monetary rights and state remedial autonomy

**Question decided:** Whether Congress may impose a substantive monetary obligation on a State under Article I and require private enforcement when the State supplies no adequate substitute remedial system.

**Holding:** Congress may validly impose a substantive monetary obligation on a State pursuant to Article I. State sovereignty permits a nonconsenting State to channel private retrospective monetary claims into its own adequate remedial system, but it does not permit the State to extinguish the federal obligation. When Congress unmistakably creates a private compensatory remedy and the State supplies no adequate substitute forum capable of enforcing the federal entitlement, a state court possessing ordinary jurisdiction over comparable claims must hear the federal action.

**Authority:** Stone’s Opinion of the Court, joined by O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, and Ginsburg, supplies a five-Justice majority. Stevens and Breyer concur in the judgment on the broader ground that Congress may authorize the FLSA action directly without first offering Maine a forum choice. Scalia and Thomas would affirm categorical immunity.

**Controlling explanation:** A state remedial system is adequate when it provides a neutral adjudicator, reasonable access, a reasonably timely determination, authority to award substantially the full federal compensatory entitlement, interest and fee treatment sufficient to prevent practical destruction of the claim where those mechanisms are necessary to enforcement, an enforceable payment obligation, and no discrimination against the claim because federal law supplies the right. The State may select the forum and ordinary procedure; it may not use that authority to make the federal entitlement nominal, discretionary, inaccessible, or unenforceable.

**Application:** The FLSA validly governs Maine as an employer and unmistakably creates the probation officers’ private compensatory remedy. The Maine courts dismissed on a categorical immunity rule and did not determine whether Maine provides an adequate alternative remedial system. That issue must be resolved on remand. If an adequate state route exists, Maine may require its use. If none exists, a Maine court with ordinary jurisdiction over comparable wage or compensation claims must adjudicate the federal action.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Maine may use ordinary limitations periods, reasonable notice rules, claims commissions, administrative tribunals, specialized state courts, and other neutral procedures that preserve meaningful enforcement. It may not substitute a nominal cap for substantially full federal compensation, make payment depend on discretionary legislative grace, impose an impossible notice deadline, assign adjudication to a tribunal controlled by the defendant agency, or deny a remedy because the right is federal. A nominal $5,000 ceiling, for example, cannot enforce an established $80,000 federal wage entitlement. Liability, limitations, the compensation due, interest, fees, and every other preserved FLSA merits issue remain unresolved. Federal public enforcement, genuine waiver, valid Reconstruction Amendment enforcement, and properly confined prospective officer relief remain independent routes.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Seminole Tribe v. Florida* is clarified. It sustained an unmistakably enacted prospective Article I action and reserved the constitutional treatment of retrospective compensatory relief; Article I may impose a monetary obligation, and state sovereignty protects remedial channeling rather than extinction of the federal right. *Garcia v. San Antonio Metropolitan Transit Authority* is reaffirmed; Congress may impose the substantive FLSA obligation on state employers. *Testa v. Katt* and *Howlett v. Rose* are applied and clarified; a State may use a neutral adequate remedial channel, but a court possessing ordinary jurisdiction over comparable claims may not refuse the federal action when no adequate substitute exists. *Wisconsin Department of Corrections v. Schacht* is applied; sovereign immunity remains claim-, defendant-, and remedy-specific rather than eliminating the federal obligation or all judicial power over the action, and its removal-jurisdiction holding remains unchanged. *Reich v. Collins*, *McKesson Corp. v. Division of Alcoholic Beverages and Tobacco*, and *South Central Bell Telephone Co. v. Alabama* are extended at the level of remedial choice: a State may select the machinery for enforcing a federal monetary entitlement, but the selected route must supply a real and adequate remedy.

### Ortiz v. Fibreboard Corp., 527 U.S. 815 (1999)

**Docket or dockets:** Not supplied in the controlling record.
**Decided:** June 23, 1999.

**Judgment:** Reversed and remanded, 7-2. Supporting: Stone, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg. Opposing: Stevens, Breyer.

**Remedy or remand:** The judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit is reversed, the mandatory class certification and settlement approval are vacated, and the case is remanded for proceedings consistent with Rule 23 and due process.

**Opinions:**

| Writing | Author | Joined by | Relationship to judgment | Scope joined |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opinion of the Court | Souter | Stone, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg | Supports reversal and remand | Complete opinion |
| Concurrence | Scalia | Kennedy | Supports reversal and remand | Rule-bound treatment of mass-tort settlement and the need for legislative or rulemaking action |
| Dissent | Breyer | Stevens | Would affirm | Complete dissent |

#### Question 1: Limited fund and adequate representation

**Question decided:** Limited fund and adequate representation.

**Holding:** A mandatory settlement class under Rule 23(b)(1)(B) requires a fund independently demonstrated to be fixed at its maximum practical value, insufficient to satisfy the aggregate claims, substantially devoted to the claimant class, and distributed equitably. Rule 23(a) also requires conflict-free representation, including separately represented subclasses when present and future claimants or other materially distinct groups have opposed interests.

**Authority:** The proposition is supported by Stone, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and is controlling.

**Controlling explanation:** Mandatory aggregation eliminates individual control and the right to opt out, so the limited-fund category must remain tied to the traditional conditions that justify binding absent claimants. The asserted limit here was derived primarily from the parties’ negotiated valuation of disputed insurance coverage rather than specific findings establishing the maximum assets practically available to satisfy claims. Fibreboard contributed little of its own net worth and retained substantial value outside the settlement. The agreement also placed currently injured claimants, exposure-only claimants, future disease claimants, and persons affected differently by insurance and payment provisions within one representation structure. Their interests diverged concerning immediate payment, inflation, latency, proof, annual limits, and the value of future claims. Post hoc fairness findings could not replace representatives whose incentives corresponded to each materially distinct group. Settlement may remove trial-management problems, but under simulated *Amchem Products v. Windsor* it does not relax Rule 23’s certification and adequacy requirements. ([Library of Congress Tiles](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep527/usrep527815/usrep527815.pdf))

**Treatment of earlier authority:** *Amchem Products, Inc. v. Windsor*: applied and extended; every Rule 23 requirement continues to govern a mandatory settlement class, and settlement cannot cure conflicting incentives among present and future claimants.

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(b)(1)(B): established; a mandatory limited-fund class requires an independently demonstrated maximum fund, aggregate insufficiency, substantial commitment of the fund, and equitable claimant treatment.

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(a)(4): clarified; materially opposed claimant groups require conflict-free representation and, when necessary, separately represented subclasses.

Rules Enabling Act: applied; Rule 23 may not be enlarged to abridge absent claimants’ substantive rights merely because mandatory aggregation would produce administrative advantages.

**Application:** The global mandatory settlement may not bind the class in its present form. The parties remain free to pursue individual settlements, narrower opt-out classes, separately represented subclasses, bankruptcy, or a genuine limited-fund proceeding satisfying the governing requirements.
